messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 62-year-old African-American stockbroker, has been struggling with intense psychological distress following the unexpected death of his brother. The shock and grief have left him feeling adrift and overwhelmed by fragmented memories that emerge without warning. These sudden pieces of memory—often just snippets of conversations or moments from the day his brother passed away—have made it hard for John to deliberately recall what happened. He often finds himself ruminating on why this event occurred, trying desperately to make sense of something he feels is still incomplete. John’s work as a stockbroker has become increasingly challenging due to these intrusive thoughts and memories. On many occasions, these fragments appear suddenly when he least expects them—during high-stakes meetings or while poring over financial reports. He often tries to suppress his thoughts about the traumatic event, but this only seems to exacerbate his distress. This difficulty in deliberately recalling what happened has left him feeling like there are significant gaps in his understanding of the tragedy. What frightens John most is that these sudden memories have also made him take unnecessary risks at work. He feels compelled to distract himself from the pain and confusion by engaging in risky financial trades, hoping that success will provide some distraction or validation. His heightened negative emotions—fear, anger, guilt—often surface unexpectedly when he experiences flashbacks during his daily routine. These intense feelings have led him to suppress thoughts about the trauma further, believing that focusing on work might shield him from the emotional pain. John’s preoccupation with these memories and his attempts to avoid grief reminders have taken a toll on his personal life as well. He has grown increasingly isolated, avoiding social gatherings or any activities that remind him of his brother. The more he tries to suppress his thoughts about the event, the harder it becomes for him to deliberately recall what happened, which in turn fuels his rumination and anxiety. The cycle continues as John’s negative emotions intensify each time a fragment of memory resurfaces, leading him to take even greater risks at work. These risky behaviors, in turn, exacerbate his feelings of guilt and shame, further deepening the trauma’s impact on his mental state. His attempts to manage these overwhelming thoughts have only led to more avoidance and confusion. John’s difficulty in deliberately recalling what happened has also reinforced his belief that something significant is missing from his understanding of the event. This incomplete picture makes it harder for him to process the grief, leaving him stuck in a cycle of rumination and flashbacks. His constant fear that he might lose control or be overwhelmed by these memories drives his risky behavior as a form of distraction. It was during one particularly stressful trading session, when a sudden memory fragment triggered a flashback and left John feeling paralyzed with fear, that he realized he needed help. He is most afraid that the trauma will continue to dominate his life, but he hopes that through therapy, he can find a way to cope more effectively with these memories and regain control over his emotions. John’s current state of mind is marked by intense distress and confusion. The overwhelming nature of his symptoms has made it clear to him that seeking professional help is necessary if he wants to break free from the cycle that has taken hold of his life.
